---
title: "Hierarchies of Worth"
---

::: {.book-page}
::: {.book-body}

*Race and the Distribution of Concern in World Politics.* Book manuscript under review.

Why do states sometimes absorb substantial costs to protect some foreign populations while treating much smaller costs as prohibitive for others? I call this inequality the distribution of concern, which is the variation in the political weight states attach to people beyond their own political communities. I develop this argument into a general theory of international hierarchy. I show that a single global hierarchy does not organize international order. Instead, it is marked by an architecture of different positions that depend on the given area of international politics.

I use a measurement model to compare countries’ positions across seven areas of international politics: diplomacy, international organizations, treaty formation, mobility, trade, cross-border banking, and investment agreements. In the 2019 data, two related dimensions emerge: state connectedness and mobility-linked access.

India, for example, occupies a favorable position in diplomatic and organizational hierarchies while its citizens occupy a considerably less favorable one in international mobility. I show that the hierarchies are remarkably durable within each area, and their racial structures vary across domains. I then show how race structures both dimensions and shapes whose claims governments treat as worth the cost.

I argue that race and racism are central to the contemporary and historical emergence of this architecture. But the results show that there is not a single global racial hierarchy. Instead, these racialized positions matter differently in different areas of international politics.
